entries.narration: Before choosing any Databricks feature, a data engineer asks what the finished data has to do for the people who use it. Every design is judged on four things those people can feel. Who reads it, how fresh it is, how correct it is, and what it costs to produce. Take one stream of retail orders and three readers. The finance team closes the books and needs daily totals by six in the morning, right to the cent. A store dashboard can show numbers about fifteen minutes old, but the counts must match what the stores see. An analyst studying history can wait until the next day, but the data must not contain the same order twice. I should be clear that these figures are assumptions I picked to show the trade-offs. They are not measurements from a real company. Now notice that the three readers pull in different directions. Fresher data means running more often, and running more often costs more. Stricter correctness means more checks, and checks take time. So one pipeline rarely suits all three equally, and the first engineering decision is deciding whose need sets the design. The common trap is believing that fresher is always better. If finance only reads a total once a day, refreshing it every fifteen minutes spends money and buys nothing. Keep these four questions, because every later chapter returns to them. Next we look at where Spark, Delta and Databricks each fit in meeting them.

Three names appear in almost every Databricks conversation, and it helps to give each one exactly one job. A lakehouse is the idea that ties them together. You keep a single copy of your data in open file formats in cloud storage, and you use that same copy for SQL analysis and for data engineering code. Apache Spark is the engine that does the computing. It splits work across machines and returns results. Delta Lake is what makes a folder of files behave like a table, by adding a transaction log beside the data files. Databricks is the platform that runs Spark and Delta for you, and adds security, governance, scheduling and the workspace you log in to. To see what Delta really is, look at the order table from our example, created in a local run of Spark four and Delta four. On disk it is two Parquet data files and a folder called delta log containing one JSON file, numbered all zeros. Inside that file the actions appear in order: a commit record, the table's metadata, the protocol versions, and two add lines naming the two data files. That commit is version zero of the table. A reader asks the log which files make up the table, and does not trust a folder listing. That is why Delta can offer reliable changes later. Two misconceptions are worth clearing now. Spark does not store your data, it only computes over files that live in storage. And Delta is not a database server, it is a table format made of files and a log. One caution: the number of data files depends on how the data was split when written, so another run could produce a different count. Next we place these pieces inside accounts, workspaces and storage.

Now let's place those pieces on a map, because the same operation touches several boundaries and each one has a different owner. At the top is the Databricks account. An account holds one or more workspaces, for example a dev workspace and a prod workspace. A workspace is the place where people work: it holds notebooks, jobs and settings. Code does not run inside the workspace page itself. It runs on compute, and compute comes in two placements. Serverless compute is managed by Databricks. Classic compute runs in your own cloud account. The data lives somewhere else again, in object storage in your cloud account, which on AWS means S3. Follow a single query to see how these fit. You open a notebook in the prod workspace and run a cell. The code runs on compute. The compute reads Delta files from object storage and returns a result. When the compute stops, the files are still exactly where they were, because storage outlives every cluster. Two misconceptions are worth naming. A workspace is not a database. It holds your notebooks and jobs, and the governed data objects are handled separately, which is the subject of the next chapter. And resizing or restarting compute never moves or deletes data. Keeping storage and compute apart in your head is what lets you reason about cost, failure and access later. Next we compare the compute choices themselves.

Compute is where your code actually runs, and Databricks offers three families. Serverless compute is managed by Databricks, so you give it work and the platform provisions and scales it. Classic compute is configured by you, in your own cloud account, so you choose things like the machine sizes and the runtime version. A SQL warehouse is compute built for SQL queries and dashboards. It also comes in serverless and classic styles. Let's make provisional choices for the retail flow. The nightly job that ingests and transforms the orders is short and bursty, so a serverless job is a reasonable first choice. The analysts and the store dashboard run SQL, so a SQL warehouse suits them. If some job needs a specific runtime or cluster level tuning, classic compute is where you get that control. I call these provisional on purpose. They are starting points, and chapter nine returns to them with real measurements. There is one belief to avoid, that serverless is always cheaper. What you pay depends on both the rate and the idle time, so the honest answer comes from comparing on your own workload. And which options you actually have depends on your workspace and region, so verify that before you depend on one. This course quotes no prices for that reason. Next we write a first query and read its result.

Here is the first real query, and the point is to read it, not to memorise it. A Databricks notebook cell sends code to compute. The compute reads a table from storage, does the work, and sends back a small result, which the notebook displays. In a Databricks notebook a Spark session called spark is already defined for you. Our table is bronze orders, with eight rows from the retail example. The question is simple: how many orders are there per status? On the left is the SQL. From bronze orders, group by status, count the rows, and sort by status. On the right is the same question in PySpark. Read the table, group by status, aggregate a count, and order by status. Both describe the same intent, and Spark plans them to the same kind of work. Underneath, Spark splits the table's files into tasks, counts in parallel, then combines the partial counts. Both return the same three rows from my local run: cancelled one, completed six, pending one. Now stop on that six, because it is the trap. Completed is six rows, not six orders. The table contains order four twice, because it was resent, and order seven, whose amount is the text n slash a. The distinct valid completed orders are one, two, four and five, which is four. A query can be perfectly correct and still answer the wrong question, if the data underneath is not ready. Fixing that is the job of the next section, where we layer the data.

The last idea in this chapter is how to organise the work. A common design is to build data in layers, usually called bronze, silver and gold. Bronze keeps what arrived, close to the source. Silver makes it trustworthy, with proper types and no duplicates. Gold answers one business question. Let's run our eight orders through all three, using a local run. Bronze holds eight raw rows, and every column is text. To build silver, I cast the store and amount to real types, keep one copy of each identical row, and refuse rows whose amount cannot be read as a decimal. Order four was resent with identical values, so it is merged. Order seven has the amount n slash a, so it is rejected. Silver has six rows. Gold takes the completed silver orders and sums them per store. Store seven has two orders totalling sixty five. Store nine has one, fifteen. Store twelve has one, eighty. Gold has three rows, and the total is one hundred and sixty. Now reconcile, because a pipeline you cannot reconcile is a pipeline you cannot trust. Eight rows in bronze equals six in silver, plus one resend, plus one rejected row. Every row is accounted for. Here is the caution that matters. A name like silver guarantees nothing by itself. Atomic writes come from Delta. Who may read comes from governance. Whether the rules are right comes from the job that wrote the table. And not every flow needs three layers. Use the pattern where it helps. The flow now needs named data objects and authorised access, so next we establish governance before ingestion.

Before we grant anyone anything, we need names for what is being protected. In Unity Catalog, governed data lives in a tree with three levels of naming. At the root is the metastore, the regional holder of the metadata. Beneath it are catalogs, beneath those are schemas, and inside a schema sit the objects themselves: tables, views and volumes. So an object's full name has three parts, catalog, schema, object. For our retail example I use a catalog called retail, with three schemas named bronze, silver and gold. The orders table from chapter one is now retail dot bronze dot orders, and its cleaned sibling is retail dot silver dot orders. You can shorten a name by setting defaults for the session. Use catalog retail and use schema silver, and then the bare name orders resolves to the same table. That is convenient in a notebook, but it depends on the session, so pipelines and jobs should use full names. Two misconceptions to clear. A name is not just a label. It is also the place where permissions attach and flow downward, which is the subject of section four. And an unqualified name is not safe, because which table it means depends on whoever's session ran it. I should be clear about the status of this chapter. There was no Unity Catalog metastore available while authoring, so every example here is documented, not run, and the names retail, bronze and so on are illustrative. Next we separate tables, views and volumes.

Now let's separate the kinds of objects, because the way you reach data decides which permission you need. A table holds rows with a schema, and you read it by its SQL name. A view is a saved query over one or more tables, and you also read it by name. A volume is a governed folder of files of any kind, such as CSV, images or JSON, and you read it by a path that starts with slash Volumes, then catalog, schema and volume name. Take the landing area of our retail example. To count rows you write a select over retail dot bronze dot orders, and that needs the select privilege. To read the raw CSV file for the first of October, you point Spark at the path under slash Volumes slash retail slash bronze slash landing, and that needs the read volume privilege. Both are governed by Unity Catalog, but by different privileges on different objects. That leads to two misconceptions. Having select on a table does not let you read files, because tables and volumes are separate objects with separate grants. And a volume is not a table of files, because it carries no schema. It is just a place for files whose structure is your business. This chapter's examples are documented, not run, so check the privilege names and path form against the current documentation. Next we ask who owns the underlying storage.

The next question is who is responsible for the files behind a table. There are two answers. A managed table keeps its files in storage that Unity Catalog manages, so the platform owns their lifecycle. An external table points at a path in your own cloud storage, so you own the lifecycle. You can tell them apart in the create statement. In our example, the silver orders table is created with no location, so it is managed. The partner feed table names an S3 path with a location clause, so it is external. The difference matters most when something is dropped. If you drop a managed table, Unity Catalog removes the underlying files after a recovery window, which the documentation puts at seven days, and I would re-check that number before relying on it. If you drop an external table, only the metadata goes. The files stay exactly where they were, and whoever owns that bucket still owns them. A common misconception is that external means ungoverned. It does not. The table is still governed, with grants and lineage. The difference is only that its files outlive it, and that you carry the storage responsibilities, such as retention and cleanup. So the practical question is what happens to storage after a drop. For managed tables, retention and cleanup follow Unity Catalog's rules. For external tables, you must delete the files yourself, or they stay and keep costing storage. The bucket name in this example is fictional, and the example is documented, not run. Next we look at who is allowed to do things to these objects.

Permissions go to principals. A principal can be a user, a group of users, or a service principal, which is an identity for automation such as a scheduled job. Prefer groups for people, so that access follows team membership rather than individuals. Privileges are granted on an object and are inherited by the objects beneath it. Grant select on a schema and it covers every table in that schema. To read a table you need three things: use catalog on its catalog, use schema on its schema, and select on the table or an ancestor. Here are the grants for our retail example. Analysts get use catalog on retail, and use schema and select on the gold schema, so they can read gold and nothing else. Data engineers get all privileges on bronze and silver. The ETL service principal can read bronze and read and write silver, and nothing more, which is least privilege: the smallest grant that lets the work happen. The matrix shows the result. And if an analyst runs a select on silver orders, it is refused, because they hold none of the three required privileges there. The error text on the board is the shape of a denial, not an exact message. Two habits make this scale. Grant to groups, so access follows team membership. And remember that a grant on the silver schema also covers tables created there later, so review grants when you add objects. One misconception to avoid is that select alone is enough. Without use catalog and use schema, the table cannot be reached. The matrix was checked against a small model of these rules, not against a live metastore, so treat this section as documented, not run. Next we connect these permissions to cloud storage.

So far, permissions have lived inside Unity Catalog. But the files themselves live in cloud storage, and the cloud has its own rules. A single read can pass through three separate controls, and any one of them can say no. The workspace decides who may open and run things. Unity Catalog decides who may read which objects. And the cloud's own identity system decides what the underlying role can actually reach. The bridge between Unity Catalog and the cloud has two parts. A storage credential wraps a cloud IAM role, and it is typically created in Catalog Explorer or through the API. An external location pairs that credential with a specific path. Our example creates an external location called partner feed, pointing at a fictional S3 path, using a credential called partner role. Then we grant read files on it to the data engineers. Now trace a read of the partner feed. Is the user allowed into the workspace? Does the user hold read files on the location? Can the IAM role behind the credential reach that path? Any single no stops the read, and the error you see depends on which control refused. The setup is done once. The credential is created from an IAM role, and each external location names the path it covers and needs its own grants. The misconception here is that grants alone are enough. If the IAM role has no access to the bucket, the read fails even when every Unity Catalog grant is perfect. That is why we explain the three controls separately. This example is documented, not run, and requires cloud-side setup. Next we see how to find and trace governed data.

Governance is not only about saying no. It is also about being able to look things up. Unity Catalog records three kinds of evidence. Metadata is the names, comments and tags that help people discover data. Lineage records which objects fed which. And audit records events, such as who accessed what. You can browse these in Catalog Explorer, and where they are enabled you can query them through system tables. Take our gold sales table. Its chain starts at the landing volume, flows into bronze orders, then silver orders, then gold sales. A query against the table lineage system table, filtering on gold sales as the target, returns its source tables. In our case that is silver orders. I want to be honest that the result row on this board is illustrative. It is not from a real run, since no workspace was available. Two caveats matter. System tables have to be enabled, and the exact column names should be checked against the current documentation. And lineage tells you what ran, not whether the logic was right. A table can have perfect lineage and still be wrong. Audit records matter for a different reason. When something goes wrong, they are the evidence of who did what and when. Next we compare ways of reaching data that lives elsewhere.

The last question in this chapter is what to do when the data you need belongs to someone else, or lives in another system. There are three broad answers. You can ingest it, which copies it into your own tables. You can use Delta Sharing, which gives you read access to a provider's data without copying it. Or you can use Lakehouse Federation, which lets you query an external database in place, through Unity Catalog. Suppose a partner has the orders we want. If we ingest, the data is as fresh as our last load, and we pay for storage and the loading compute. If the partner shares it with us, we read their live data, and our own compute runs the query. If we federate to their database, we read live from the source, and the source system carries the query load. So choose by asking four things. How fresh must it be? Who pays to read it? May the data leave where it lives? And how much load can the source take? Two misconceptions follow. No copy does not mean no cost, because compute, source load and, across regions or clouds, data transfer can all add up. And federation does not replace ingestion, because a busy operational database may not tolerate analytical queries. This is a comparison, with no prices quoted, and it is documented, not run. Governance defines who can access data. Next we explain the table semantics that make changes reliable.

Chapter one showed that a Delta table is data files plus a transaction log. Now let's see precisely how the log defines the table. Every change to the table is a commit, and each commit appends one JSON file to the delta log folder, numbered in order. Inside that file are actions. An add action says a data file is now part of the table. A remove action says a data file no longer is. The metadata action carries the schema. To know what the table contains at some version, you replay the log up to that version and see which files are left. That set of files is a snapshot. Data files themselves are never edited. Here is our silver orders table in a local run of Spark four and Delta four. Version zero is the create, with only metadata and protocol actions. Version one writes the six orders, version two adds order eight, so the table now has seven rows. Version three updates order six, and version four deletes order three. Both of those commits contain a remove and an add. That tells you what really happened: the file holding those rows was rewritten as a new file, and the old one was marked removed. The sixth commit, version five, is a merge, and it leaves seven rows. A misconception is that an update changes the file in place. It does not. The old file stays on disk, still reachable through older versions, until something vacuums it, which is section six. That is the trade: kept old files make history and time travel possible, and they are also why storage grows until a vacuum. Next we ask what happens when two writers commit at once.

Delta advertises ACID transactions, and the useful question is what that actually covers. Start with atomicity. A commit works by adding one new log file. Either that file appears whole, or it does not appear, so a reader sees a complete version of the table and never half a write. Next, concurrency. Delta uses optimistic concurrency: each writer assumes nobody else is conflicting, does its work against the snapshot it read, and then checks at commit time. Let's force a real conflict in a local run. Writer A starts an update on order one, reads version one, and scans slowly. Meanwhile writer B updates the amount on order one, and commits version two. When A finally tries to commit, Delta refuses, with a concurrent append exception telling it the table changed and to try again. After that, order one has amount forty one and status completed. A's change to the status was not applied. Contrast that with two plain inserts at the same moment. Both committed, because adding unrelated rows does not conflict. This design means nobody takes a lock, so readers and unrelated writers are never blocked. Now the limits. The guarantee covers one table per commit. And a refused writer does not retry on its own. Your application, or the job that runs it, must decide to retry, and it must be safe to run twice. Error codes and wording can differ on Databricks. Next we look at what Delta does when the data itself does not match the table.

Data arrives in shapes we did not plan for, so a table has to decide what to accept. Delta enforces the table's schema when you write. If the data does not fit, the write is refused, and the table is left exactly as it was. Changing the schema is possible, but you have to ask for it. That is called schema evolution. On top of types, you can add rules. A not null declaration and a check constraint turn a business rule into something the table itself enforces. That is a data contract: a promise about what the table will contain, checked at the door. Here are five writes against a small copy of the orders table, run locally. A row with an extra column is refused, and the message tells you to set merge schema if you meant it. Putting the text a b c into an integer column is refused as an invalid cast. A null order id is refused by the not null rule. An amount of minus five is refused by the check constraint, which is named positive amount. Finally, an append that carries a new channel column with the merge schema option set is accepted. The table gains a channel column, and the older rows simply read null for it. The misconception is that evolution happens by itself. It does not. Without the option, that extra column is an error, which is exactly what protects downstream readers. One note: in this local version I declared not null when creating the table, because adding it later was refused. Next we look at the statements that change rows.

Four statements change rows in a Delta table: insert, update, delete and merge. Each one commits a new version. Merge is the most powerful, and the most often misread, so let's be precise about it. A merge joins a source to the target table on a condition. For each row it asks whether there is a match, and then applies the action you wrote for that case. In our example, the source is a small table of updates holding two orders. Order eight is already in the table as pending, and the update marks it completed. Order nine is not in the table at all. The on condition compares order ids. Order eight matches, so the matched clause runs and its status changes from pending to completed. Order nine does not match, so the not matched clause runs and it is inserted. The table history for that commit confirms it: one row updated and one row inserted. Now the rule that catches people. If two source rows both match the same target row, merge raises an error. In the local run it reported that multiple source rows matched one target row. It never silently picks one, which is a good thing, because picking one would make the result depend on row order. So before you merge, make your source unique on the match key. So make the source unique on the key first, for example by keeping the latest row per key. That is why deduplication comes before merge in later chapters. Next we look at the history those commits leave behind.

Because every commit stays in the log, a Delta table remembers its past, and there are three related things you can do with that. You can list the history, which shows each version and its operation. You can time travel, which means reading the table as of an older version, with version as of and a number. And you can restore, which means making the table match an older version again. The difference between the last two is the one worth remembering. Time travel only reads. Nothing changes. Restore writes: it adds a brand new commit that brings the table back to the earlier state. In our local run, the merge at version five left seven rows, and suppose we decide it was wrong. We restore the table to version four. That creates version six, and the table has six rows again. Notice what did not happen. Version five is still in the history, and reading version five still returns seven rows. So the misconception to avoid is that restore erases history. It adds to it, and the table is back, but the record of what happened stays. So use time travel to inspect or compare a past state, and restore to undo a bad change. There is a catch, though, and it is the subject of the next section. Both time travel and restore depend on the old data files still being there. If those files have been removed, the past is no longer readable. Next we look at retention and vacuum.

Time travel and restore are not free, and they are not permanent. When a file is replaced by an update or a delete, the old file stays on disk so that older versions can still be read. That costs storage. The command that reclaims it is vacuum. Vacuum deletes data files that no current version needs and that are older than the retention period. Once those files are gone, the versions that used them can no longer be read. Here is a throwaway table in a local run. It has three versions: two ids, then a third added, then the first deleted. Before vacuum, all three versions read fine. Then I ran vacuum with a retention of zero hours. To do that I had to switch off a safety check, because by default Delta refuses a retention shorter than seven days. After the vacuum, versions one and two fail with a file not exist error. Version three and the current table still read, because the files they need are still there. The documented defaults are seven days for removed files and thirty days for the commit log, and I would verify them on your platform. The trade-off is plain. Longer retention gives you more ability to recover and more storage cost. And a reader or a stream that needs data older than the retention can fail. So retention should be chosen on purpose, to match the longest reader or recovery window you promise. Next we look at recording changes themselves.

Delta can also tell you what changed, row by row. If you enable the change data feed on a table, each commit also records its row level changes: inserts, deletes, and for updates both a before image and an after image. Each change carries the commit version it came from. Here is a small table in a local run, with the feed switched on by a table property. Version one inserts orders one and two. Version two updates order one from pending to completed, and the feed shows that as two rows: the pre image and the post image. Version three deletes order two. Reading the feed from version one returns five change rows. Two boundaries matter. First, the feed only exists from the moment it is enabled. On a second table where I enabled it later, asking for a version before that point failed with a missing change data error. Second, the changes are stored in a folder beside the data and are subject to retention, so a vacuum can remove them. That is why the feed is not an archive. It is also not the same thing as change data capture from a source system. It sees this table's commits, not the events the source produced. This example uses the feed configured by a table property. Whether Databricks provides one automatically for some tables is a platform behaviour I did not run, so check the current documentation. Next we look at compatibility.

A Delta table is read and written by many kinds of clients, and they are not all equally new. The table's protocol is how it says what a client must understand. It records a minimum reader version, a minimum writer version, and a set of named table features. Using a feature can raise those numbers. Let's read them from three tables in a local run, using describe detail. A plain table has reader version one and writer version two. When I added a check constraint to another table, its writer version became three, and a feature called check constraints appeared. When I enabled the change data feed on a third table, its writer version became seven, and the feature list included change data feed. Every table also listed append only and invariants. The practical meaning is that a client older than the protocol may be unable to write the table, or in some cases to read it. Now, Delta is an open format, but the platform around it moves at its own pace. Databricks adds features and has runtime requirements for them, and which ones apply depends on the runtime and the feature. I could not run the platform, so treat any platform specific feature as documented, not run. Before you enable something, ask which clients must still work, whether it raises the protocol, and whether another engine needs to read the table. We now have a governed, transactional destination. Next we bring source data into it incrementally and account for imperfect inputs.

Before writing any ingestion code, write down what the source promises. Call it a source contract. It names the format, the key, how data arrives, whether records can repeat, and how long the source keeps them. Everything the pipeline does later leans on those answers. Take our retail order files. They are CSV files with a header row, and the key is the order id. They arrive one at a time. In this example there are three files, with three, three and two rows. Notice that order four appears twice, in the second and third files, so a repeat is possible, and the design has to have a rule for it. Finally, retention. I assumed the source keeps files for thirty days. That is an assumption for the example, not a measurement, and it matters because it sets how far back you could ever replay. The questions on the board are the ones to ask a source owner. Can a key repeat, and across files? Can old files change or disappear? How long can I replay? And who will tell me when the format changes? Also record who owns the source and how changes are announced, and whether old files can be corrected or replaced after the fact. A misconception worth naming is that the source is the source of truth. It is the source of truth only for what it still holds, and only to the extent it keeps its promises. Next we load these files in bulk.

The simplest way to ingest is a batch load: read a named set of files, once, and write them into a table. On Databricks, the SQL command for this is copy into. Its documented behaviour is that it remembers which files it has already loaded, and skips them if you run it again. I could not run it here, so treat that as documented, not run. What I could run is the plain alternative. Reading the same eight rows from the three files and appending them to a table gives eight rows. Running the same append a second time gives sixteen, because a plain append has no memory of what it read. So the first assumption to check in any load is what happens when it runs twice. Jobs get retried, people click run again, and a load that is not repeat safe quietly doubles your data. The second assumption is scope. Copy into loads the files in the path you name. Files that are changed or added outside that path are simply not seen. The misconception to avoid is that re-running a load is safe. It is safe only if the load tracks what it has already read. Next we look at the source that does this tracking for you incrementally.

Auto Loader is how Databricks ingests files incrementally. It is a Structured Streaming source called cloud files. Instead of re-reading everything, it discovers the files that are new in a storage location and processes each one once. It also adds schema tracking, and it can keep data that does not fit the schema instead of dropping it. This board is documented, not run, because Auto Loader is a Databricks source and I had no workspace. So re-check the option names against the current documentation. Read the code from the top. Format cloud files names the source, and the cloud files format option says the files are CSV. The schema location option says where Auto Loader keeps the schema it has inferred. The load path is a volume path. On the write side, the checkpoint location says where progress is kept. The trigger, available now, means process everything that is there, then stop, which suits a scheduled job. And to table writes into a governed Delta table. The misconception to avoid is that this is some separate engine. It is a Spark stream source, so the same ideas about checkpoints and restarts apply, and the next section shows them in a local run. Next we see how progress is tracked.

Incremental ingestion works because something remembers what has already been read. For a stream, that memory is the checkpoint. Let me show it with Spark's own file stream source in a local run. This is the closest analogue I could run, and Auto Loader's internals are documented, not run. Run one starts with file a, three rows, and bronze has three. Run two finds file b, adds three, and bronze has six. Run three is a restart with nothing new, and it adds nothing. That is the point of the checkpoint: restarting does not re-read. Run four finds file c and adds two, for a total of eight. Now run five, where I deleted the checkpoint and ran again. The query had no memory, so it read all three files again and appended eight more rows. Bronze now has sixteen. Looking inside the checkpoint folder, there is a metadata file holding the query's identity, an offsets folder of what each batch planned, and a commits folder of what each batch finished. Why is a restart safe? Offsets are written before a batch runs and committed after it finishes, so a crash between the two simply re-runs that batch. So who owns this? One checkpoint belongs to one query writing to one sink. Do not share it between queries, move it casually, or delete it. In declarative pipelines, which we reach in chapter seven, the platform manages this state for you, and that is documented rather than run here. Next we deal with files that change shape.

Sources change, and when they do, what happens depends on how you read them. Here are two small JSON files from a local run. The first is a normal order. The second has two surprises: the amount is the text twelve comma fifty, in the European style, and there is a new field called channel. Read them with a fixed schema, and two things happen silently. The new channel field is simply not there. And, more worrying, the text twelve comma fifty was parsed as one thousand two hundred fifty, with no error and no flag. The comma was treated as a thousands separator. That is a wrong value, delivered quietly. Now read them with schema inference instead. The amount column is inferred as a string, because it must hold both forms, and channel is a string. Read the first file alone and the amount was inferred as a double. So with inference, a column's type can change underneath you when an odd file arrives. Neither read raised an error. That is the lesson. A fixed schema protects the table but can hide drift, and inference follows the data but can change types. Auto Loader offers evolution modes that make the choice explicit: add new columns, rescue unexpected data, fail on new columns, or ignore changes. Those are documented, not run, so check the names. Next we look at keeping data that cannot be read.

A pipeline that silently drops a record it cannot read has lost data, and nobody knows. The safer habit is to keep what you could not parse, with its original text, and to prove that every row is accounted for. In a local run, I read the three order files with a typed schema in permissive mode, and asked Spark to keep the raw text of any record that failed in a column called bad record. Eight rows were read. Order seven has the amount n slash a, which cannot be a decimal, so its amount became null and its original line, o seven, nine, n slash a, completed, was kept in the bad record column. Everything else parsed. Now reconcile. Eight rows read equals seven parsed plus one flagged. And notice that the seven good rows still include the resent order four, because removing duplicates is a different job, which comes in the next chapter. A flagged row goes to quarantine, a place where someone can look at it and decide what to do. It needs the raw line, the file it came from and when it arrived, and it needs an owner who decides whether to fix it, replay it or discard it. Databricks has a related feature, a column named rescued data, which collects fields that were unexpected or did not match. I did not run it, and it works differently from this option, so read its documentation before relying on it. Next we look at managed connectors.

Sometimes you do not need to write the ingestion code at all. Databricks offers managed connectors, including Lakeflow Connect, which read from a supported source for you and keep their own progress state. I did not run any of these, so this is a comparison of responsibilities, documented, not run, and it is deliberately generic. Look at the board. If you write the ingestion yourself, you read the source, you keep the checkpoint, you choose how schema changes are handled, and you tune how much load you put on the source. With a managed connector, the connector reads the source and tracks progress, and schema handling and limits follow the connector's own rules. In both cases, you still govern the resulting tables. Permissions, ownership and lineage are still your responsibility. Compare the effort to build and run your own against the connector, not only a price. So how do you choose? Ask whether the source is supported at all. Ask what the connector cannot do. And ask how much load it may place on the source system, because a connector that runs against a busy operational database has a cost there. The misconception is that managed means no limits. Supported sources, features and limits vary by connector, so read the current documentation for the specific one. Next we look at sources that are streams of messages.

Files are one kind of source. Others are streams of messages, such as a message bus, or the change log of a database. They all share one idea. To resume, the pipeline needs a position: for files, the files already seen. For a message bus, an offset for each partition. For a database log, a position in the log. That position is stored in your checkpoint. The second shared idea is retention. A source only keeps data for so long, and that limits how far back a replay can go. This board is documented, not run, since I had no message broker. The code is the standard shape of a Kafka read. It names a source, a topic to subscribe to, and a starting offset of earliest, which means begin from the oldest retained message. The broker settings are placeholders. Now the assumptions to state out loud. Offsets live in your checkpoint, so losing the checkpoint loses your place, as we saw in the file example. If the source's retention expires before you read the data, it cannot be replayed. And delivery guarantees depend on both the source and the sink, so never say a pipeline is exactly once without naming which pair you mean. Next we put these ideas together in a first bronze table.

Now let's put the chapter together in the first bronze table. Bronze keeps what arrived, as it was sent, with a trail back to where it came from. In our example, the three files hold three, three and two rows, so bronze holds eight rows. Those eight rows carry seven distinct order ids, because order four was resent in the third file. Each row also records its source file, taken from the file metadata, so any row can be traced to the file that brought it. The board also shows an ingested at timestamp. That is a design choice I recommend, and it was not part of my run. Two operations can change those counts. A backfill loads history that the pipeline has not seen. A replay re-reads input it already read, for example after a lost checkpoint. Both can duplicate rows. In the local run, replaying every file into the same table gave sixteen rows, eight of them copies, and nothing in a plain append stopped it. So the guard has to be designed. You can key the load, or deduplicate afterwards, and we do both in later chapters. So make loads repeat safe, record the source file on every row, and count in and out at every hop. For now, the useful habit is counting in and counting out. Three files, eight rows, seven distinct orders. Raw arrival is accounted for. Next we turn it into correct and useful business records.

Before we transform data, we need just enough of the Spark model to read what happens. The data is split into partitions, and different tasks work on different partitions at the same time. Most of the code you write does not run when you write it. A transformation, like filter or group by, only adds a step to a plan. Nothing is computed until an action asks for a result, such as collect, count, or a write. Then Spark runs the whole plan as a job. Let's count the eleven event rows in our retail bronze table, in a local run. I built the status counts, and no job had started. Then I called collect, which is an action, and a job ran. The plan Spark printed is trimmed here for readability. It shows a partial count on each partition, then a step called exchange hash partitioning on status, then a final count. That exchange is the shuffle. To count per status, all the rows with the same status have to end up in the same place, so Spark moves data between partitions. Shuffles are the expensive step to watch in later chapters. The result is cancelled one, completed eight, pending two. Notice that eight completed is rows, not orders, because the table still has resends and bad rows. The misconception to avoid is that each line runs as written. Only an action runs the plan. The Apache Spark course covers the full model, so here I only use what I need. Next we see that SQL and the DataFrame API describe the same plan.

On Databricks you will see the same transformation written in SQL and in PySpark, and it helps to know they are two spellings of one request. Both are parsed into the same kind of plan, and Spark optimises that plan before running it. So the choice between them is mostly about readability. Here is one question, asked both ways in a local run. How many completed event rows are there per store? In SQL we write where status equals completed, group by store id, and order by store id. In PySpark we write filter, group by, aggregate a count, and order by. Both return the same four rows: store seven has three, store nine has three, store twelve has one, and store fifteen has one. The four counts add up to eight, the completed rows from section one, which is a useful cross check. I also compared the two physical plans, and apart from the internal expression ids, which differ between any two queries, they are identical. That equivalence matters in review: compare either spelling to the intent, and moving a step from SQL to PySpark should not change the results. So how should you choose? SQL reads well for set logic, such as joins and aggregation. DataFrames suit steps you build programmatically, such as a list of columns or a loop. Pick one per step and keep the intent visible, and do not assume one is faster. Next we look at the assumptions inside the data itself: types, nulls, time zones and nesting.

Many wrong numbers in a data pipeline come from an assumption nobody stated, and none of them raise an error. Here are four, from a local run. First, parsing. Casting the text n slash a to a decimal safely gives null. But minus five parses perfectly well as a number. So being able to parse a value is not the same as the value being valid, and that is a separate check. Second, null. Comparing a column to null with an equals sign matches no rows at all, because null is not equal to anything, not even null. Using is null matched the one row we expected. Third, time. The text nine fourteen, with no zone, becomes an instant only when you read it in a time zone. Read in UTC and in New York, the same text gives two instants fourteen thousand four hundred seconds apart, which is four hours. So say which zone you mean. Fourth, nested data. An order has an amount and a list of line items. Exploding the line items gives one row per item, so an order level amount repeats. Summing it after the explode turned sixty five into one hundred and five. Test each of these by counting rows before and after each step, and by comparing a total to a figure you already trust. The rule of thumb is to say the time zone, the type and the grain out loud before you aggregate. Next we meet the same problem again, in joins.

A join returns one row for every matching pair. If the key is unique on one side, the other side keeps the number of rows it had. If the key repeats, the rows multiply, and any total built on them is inflated. Here is a local example from our retail data. We have five completed orders worth one hundred and seventy dollars in all. Join them to the clean stores table, where each store appears once, and you get five rows and one hundred and seventy. Now suppose the stores reference file was sent twice, so York, store nine, appears two times. The same join returns six rows and a total of one hundred and eighty five. Order four, fifteen dollars from store nine, was counted twice. Nothing raised an error. The query is valid, the types are right, and the answer is wrong by fifteen. The defence is to check the key before the join. A query that groups the reference table by store id and keeps only groups with more than one row returns store nine with a count of two, which tells you the key is not unique. Then you decide what to do about it, and re-run to confirm five rows and one hundred and seventy again. Then you decide what to do about it: remove the duplicate, or reject the file. The habit is to know the grain of both sides of every join, and to reconcile the output total to a known figure. Next we handle duplicates in the events themselves.

Events can repeat, and updates arrive as new events, so before analysis we usually keep one row per order: the latest. A window function does this. We partition the rows by order id, order them by event time, latest first, and number them with row number. Rank one is the row to keep. Look at our two examples, from a local run. Order six has two events, pending at nine twenty three and completed at nine forty one. The later one gets rank one, so we keep completed, which is the right current status. Order four is different. Its resend has exactly the same event time as the original, so they tie. If we order only by time, the database is free to choose either one, and which it chooses can depend on how the rows happen to be arranged. I tested this. I took four tied rows from four different files and shuffled their order twelve times. Ordering by time alone kept different files depending on the shuffle. Adding source file as a second sort key made it keep the same one every time, file c in our example. For identical rows the business result is the same either way, but a different row surviving can change a metadata column, and for rows that are not identical it can change the answer. Two more cautions. For the first event rather than the latest, order ascending. And filter invalid rows before ranking, or an invalid row could take rank one. So the rule is to give every deduplication a total order. A tie decided by row order is a bug waiting for a rerun. Next we put quality rules around all this.

Now let's put quality rules in front of the silver table. A rule is a test that a row either passes or fails. Rows that fail go to quarantine, kept with a reason, and rows that pass continue. And then we reconcile, which means showing that every input row ended up in exactly one place. Here are our eleven event rows, in a local run, against four rules. Is the amount readable? Order seven fails, because its amount is the text n slash a. Is the amount positive? Order eight fails, because its amount is minus five. Is the store known? Order nine fails, because store fifteen is not in the reference table. And is the status one of the allowed values? Nothing fails that. So three rows are quarantined, each with its reason, and eight rows pass. Of those eight, order four appears twice and order six appears twice, so keeping the latest per order leaves six rows. Now the reconciliation. Eleven equals six silver orders, plus one identical resend of order four, plus one superseded earlier event for order six, plus three quarantined rows. Every row is somewhere. Quarantine should keep the original values, the reason, the source file and the time, and it needs an owner and a way to replay after a fix. There is also a boundary to be clear about. A rule can say a row is valid. It cannot say the row is right. Silver is checked for valid structure here, and the business meaning is checked when we build gold. Next we shape the output for the people who read it.

A gold table is a promise to the people who read it, so it should say exactly what it contains. The first thing to declare is the grain: what does one row represent? Here, one row per store. Next come the dimensions, which describe the row, here the store id and the store name. And then the measures, which are the numbers that get counted or summed. In our table, orders counts the completed orders, and sales sums the amount over those completed orders. Writing those definitions down is a data contract, and part of it can be enforced by the table itself. In a local run I created the gold sales table with a comment on each column, and I added a check constraint saying sales can never be negative. The result has three rows. Leeds has three orders worth seventy five. York has one, worth fifteen. Hull has one, worth eighty. The total is one hundred and seventy. Be honest about what is enforced and what is not. The check constraint is enforced. The definition that only completed orders count lives in the comment and in your documentation, and a reader has to trust it. That is why the next section reconciles the summary back to the detail. Next we assemble the whole flow.

Let's run the whole flow once, with all the habits from this chapter. We start with eleven raw event rows in bronze, as text. Three fail the quality rules and are quarantined. The rest are typed and deduplicated by keeping the latest event per order, with a tie breaker, and that leaves six silver orders. In silver, five of those orders are completed, and their amounts add up to one hundred and seventy. Gold joins them to the store reference table, which has a unique key, and summarises per store. Gold has five orders and one hundred and seventy dollars. So detail equals summary, which is the reconciliation that tells you the join and the grouping did not lose or duplicate anything. You may remember that chapter one ended with a gold total of one hundred and sixty. The difference is ten dollars. In chapter one, order six was still pending. Here, a later event completed it, and that is what the latest per order logic picked up. This reference to customer attributes in the plan's title is covered by the store reference join, since our retail sample carries stores rather than customers. The three quarantined rows are not lost, they wait for a fix, and every layer's count is explained by the layer before it. The habits to keep are typed columns, rules with reasons, a total order for deduplication, unique keys on reference data, and a reconciliation at every hop. Batch transformations now define the intended results. Next we explain how those results stay correct as events and source records change.

Every pipeline answers a question at some point in time, and there are two basic ways to keep the answer current. You can recompute everything from scratch each time, or you can process only what is new and combine it with what you already know. Full recomputation is simple, and it is always consistent with the source, because it looks at everything. Incremental processing reads only new input, and keeps state so it can combine it with earlier results. Here is the difference in a local run with four files of order events, holding three, three, two and two rows. If we recompute after each file, we read three rows, then six, then eight, then ten, which is twenty seven row reads in total. Incrementally, we read three, three, two and two, which is ten. The saving grows as the history grows. But incremental processing quietly assumes things that recomputation does not. It assumes new data arrives as new rows. It assumes old rows never change. It assumes late rows have a plan, and that after a restart the query knows where it stopped. Real data breaks each of those. Orders get resent, updated and deleted, and events arrive late. So this chapter tests those assumptions one at a time, with real runs. Next we start with time, and what late data means.

Time is the hardest part of streaming, because there are two kinds. Event time is when something actually happened, as recorded in the data. Processing time is when Spark happened to see it. Events can arrive out of order, so a query that sums per window of event time has to decide when a window is finished. The tool for that is the watermark. Its value is the newest event time seen so far, minus the delay you declare, here ten minutes, and it never moves backwards. Here is a local run of ten order events in four files, with ten minute windows, in append mode, one file per batch. The watermark in force went from nothing, to nine oh four, then nine thirteen, nine twenty one, and nine thirty four. Append mode writes each window once, when the watermark passes its end. So window nine o'clock was written at batch two with ninety five, and window nine ten at batch three with one hundred and ten. The last batch had no data and ran only to advance the watermark. Now the two late events. Order ten, with event time nine oh six, arrived late but was still counted, because its window was still open. Order twelve, at nine oh two, arrived a batch later and was dropped. Without a watermark, order twelve is counted, but the state never shrinks. Read the guarantee carefully. Data within the delay is never dropped. Data later than that may or may not be counted. Next we look at the size of that state.

A stateful streaming query has to remember things. A windowed sum keeps a row for every window that is still open. A deduplication keeps a row for every key it has seen, so it can recognise a repeat. The question to ask of any stateful query is whether that memory is bounded. In a local run on the same four files, I measured the number of state rows after each batch. A windowed sum with no watermark held two, then three, four and five rows. It only grew, because no window is ever known to be finished. With a ten minute watermark the counts were two, three, three, three and two, because windows closed and left the state. Deduplication tells the same story. Dropping duplicates on order id and event time with no watermark kept three, five, seven, then nine rows, one per distinct key, forever. With a watermark it went three, three, four, three, one, because keys older than the watermark expired. That expiry is not free. It is also what dropped order twelve as late. So the trade is plain. A watermark bounds your state and costs you late data. And a deduplication key with no time component can never expire, so on an unbounded stream its state grows without limit. Choose the delay by how late your data really arrives. Next we join two streams.

Joining a stream to something else raises a new question: what must be remembered? The easy case is a stream joined to a static table, such as the store reference data. Spark reads the reference table when it needs it, and keeps no state for the stream. In our run, joining the order events to store names gave Hull two, Leeds five, and York three. A join of two streams is harder. An order and its payment may arrive in different batches, so Spark has to buffer each side until a match can no longer arrive. To keep that buffer bounded you need two things: a watermark on each side, and a time condition in the join, here that the payment comes within fifteen minutes of the order. In the local run, the inner join found orders one and two in batch zero. In batch one it found order four twice, because the order was resent and each copy matched the payment, and also order five. Order ten never matched, because its payment came twenty four minutes after the order, outside the bound. A left outer join is where you see the cost of bounded state. Order ten was emitted with a null payment only in the last batch, after the watermark had passed, because until then a match was still possible. An outer result is delayed because a match could still arrive until the watermark passes. So duplicates upstream multiply here, and outer results are delayed by design. Next we look at restarting a query.

The checkpoint is what lets a streaming query survive a restart, and it also binds the query to its state. If you restart the same query, it resumes from the checkpoint. In a local run, I ran a windowed sum over two files, stopped, added two more files, and started the same query again with the same checkpoint. It resumed at batch three and processed only the new files. Nothing was read twice. Now suppose you change the query, which will happen. I tried three changes on the same checkpoint. Adding a stateless filter was accepted. Changing the window from ten minutes to five minutes was also accepted, with no error at all. And adding store id as a grouping key was refused, with a state store key schema not compatible error, because the stored state no longer fits. The middle one is the instructive result. The checkpoint checks that the state's schema still matches. It does not check that the old state still means what the new query assumes. The window change passed because the types matched, not because the change was safe. So the rule is that no error is not the same as no problem. Any change that touches state needs thought, and often a new checkpoint with a deliberate backfill. Next we look at what a restart can do to the sink.

Even with a checkpoint, a restart can write the same rows twice, and the reason is the order of events. When you use for each batch, Spark runs your function for a batch, and only after it returns does Spark record the batch as committed. If the process dies between those two moments, then on restart Spark replays the batch, and your function runs again on the same data. So the guarantee to your sink is at least once. To see this, I made the function crash on purpose after it wrote batch two, in a local run. There were ten source rows, nine of them distinct, because the source itself resent order four. I wrote every batch to two sinks. One was a plain append, and the other was a merge keyed on order id and event time. After the crash, the append sink held eight rows and the merge sink seven. After the restart, which replayed batch two, the append sink held twelve rows, including two replayed copies, while the merge sink held nine, the correct number. A merge keyed on the data is idempotent, which means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. That is the fix. When someone says a pipeline is exactly once, ask which source and which sink they mean, because the guarantee comes from the pair, and from your function being idempotent. Next we look at changes coming from a source system.

Change data capture means the source sends you a record for each change it made: a key, an operation, which is insert, update or delete, and a sequence number from the source that says what order the changes happened in. The critical point is that the order the records arrive in is not the source's order. Here is a feed of eight records in three batches, from a local run. In batch one, three orders are inserted. In batch two, order one is updated to completed with sequence three, order two is updated, and order three is deleted. Batch three brings two late records: an older update for order one, with sequence two, and a repeat of order three's original insert. Now apply them in arrival order, with hard deletes and no sequence check. Order one ends up back at pending, because the older update arrived last and overwrote the newer one. And order three, which was deleted, comes back, because the late insert found no row and created one. Both are wrong, and neither raised an error. Applied by sequence, a record only changes a row if its sequence is greater than the one already stored. Deletes are kept as a marker rather than removed, so a late insert cannot bring the row back. A marker works because a hard delete forgets the key, while a marker with its sequence remembers it. Then order one is completed, and order three stays deleted. Next we keep not just the latest state but the history.

Once changes are applied correctly, you decide what to keep. The two classic answers are called slowly changing dimension type one and type two. Type one overwrites. You keep one current row per key, and history is lost. Type two keeps every version of a row, each with a start and an end, so you can answer what was true at some earlier point. Take the same events from the last section, deduplicated to seven distinct records. As type one, we keep the newest non deleted row per order. Order one is forty five dollars and completed, order two is twenty five and completed, and order three is gone. As type two, order one has three versions, pending at sequence one, pending with the new amount at sequence two, and completed from sequence three, which is still open. Order two has two versions. Order three has one version, which ends at sequence two where it was deleted. A delete closes the previous version and is not a version itself. Notice how the history is built. We order each key's events by sequence, and each version ends where the next begins, so the order in which records arrived cannot scramble it. Type two has a cost: six history rows for three orders, and queries that must pick the version valid at the time they ask about. Use type one when you only need the current view. Use type two when past values must stay correct, for example reporting last quarter's figures as they were. Chapter seven shows how declarative pipelines express these. Next we compare this with the table's own change feed.

People often treat the change feed of a Delta table as if it were the same thing as change data capture from the source. They answer different questions. Source CDC says what the source did, in the source's order. The table's change feed says what this table changed, one commit at a time. Here is a local example, using a feed that is configured with a table property. I applied the three batches of source records to a table with a sequence guard, and then read the table's change feed. The source had sent eight records. The feed contains nine rows. Batch one produced three inserts. Batch two produced six rows, because each of its three updates appears as a before image and an after image, even the delete, which I stored as a marker update. Batch three's two late records were ignored by the guard, so they changed nothing and left no row in the feed at all. So you cannot rebuild the source's record of events from the table's feed, because intent and order are not there. And neither feed is a permanent archive. Both are subject to retention, which the next section demonstrates. One more thing I want to be clear about. This example uses a configured feed. Databricks documents tables that can provide a feed automatically, but I did not test that, so I make no claim about it. Next we put the whole recovery story together.

Let's finish the chapter with a recovery you could trust. The core of it is one statement: a merge that applies a source record only when its sequence is greater than the one already stored, and that keeps deletes as markers. That one rule makes the apply idempotent and independent of arrival order, and I tested both in a local run. Applying all three batches twice left exactly the same table. Applying them in reverse order left exactly the same table. A late insert for order three, which had already been deleted, did not bring it back, because the delete marker has a higher sequence. Those are the failures the guard handles. There is one it cannot. I vacuumed the table with a retention of zero hours, and then tried to read its change feed from version one. The read failed, because the files were gone. A guard cannot recover rows that nobody kept. If the history you need is beyond your retention, whether that is the table's, the source's or a stream's, the recovery is to reload from a snapshot of the source, and then resume. Know the retention of the source, the stream and the tables, and whether a snapshot reload is practical, before you need it. So retention decides how far back you can replay, and you should know that number before you need it. The change processing rules are now explicit. Next we express them through managed declarative pipeline abstractions.

So far we have written streaming and merge logic by hand. A declarative pipeline lets you state each dataset as a query, and leaves the plumbing to the platform. In an imperative application, you start the stream, choose the checkpoint path, decide the order of steps, and handle the retries. In a declarative pipeline, you write something like create or refresh streaming table, followed by a query, and the platform works out the order, keeps the checkpoints, retries failures, and runs the updates. Look at the same ingestion written both ways on the board. The application wires up a stream, a checkpoint path and a sink. The pipeline is a single statement over the read files function. I want to be clear about the status of this chapter. I had no Databricks workspace, so every pipeline example is documented, not run, and I checked names against documentation search summaries only. Please verify them on the live docs before publishing. Whichever style you use, the business logic, such as the quality rules and the keys, is still yours. A word about naming. The current name is Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines. Older material calls it Delta Live Tables, or DLT, and uses an import called dlt, and I mention those only so you recognise them. Next we look at the kinds of dataset a pipeline can contain.

A pipeline is made of datasets, and there are three kinds with different jobs. A streaming table reads a stream and processes each piece of input once. That makes it the natural choice for ingestion and for steps that only append. A materialized view stores the result of a query, and the platform keeps it up to date, so it suits summaries and joins. A view stores nothing. It is a named query, computed when something reads it, and it is useful for sharing a step inside the pipeline. In the retail pipeline, bronze orders is a streaming table that appends each new file once. Typed orders is a view, a reusable step that casts the text columns. And gold sales is a materialized view that summarises the silver table. The code shows how each is declared, though it is documented, not run. Two misconceptions. A materialized view is not a table that you write rows into. It is defined by its query, and you do not insert into it. And a view does not save compute. It saves storage, because the query runs again every time it is read. So choose by responsibility: streaming tables for ingestion and append only steps, materialized views for results that must stay current, and views for steps you want to name and reuse. Next we see how these datasets connect.

In a pipeline you never write down which step must run before which. The dependencies come from what each dataset reads. A flow is a query that feeds a target dataset, and the pipeline looks at what each flow reads, builds a graph, and runs the flows in dependency order. Here is the graph for the retail example. The landing volume feeds bronze orders. Bronze orders feeds the typed orders view. The view feeds silver orders. And silver orders feeds the gold sales materialized view. The way you create each edge is simply by naming what you read. Reading from stream of bronze orders makes a streaming dependency. Reading from silver orders makes a dependency on its stored result. If the graph has a cycle, or a name is missing, the pipeline tells you before it runs anything. By default the target of a flow is a table inside the pipeline. Pipelines also document other kinds of sinks, for example for writing out to other systems, but that is a separate feature. I did not run it, so check its availability and limits before designing around it. The practical benefit is that adding a dataset is adding a query. You do not edit a schedule. Next we put quality rules on those datasets.

Chapter five wrote quality rules as filters. A pipeline gives them a name and a policy. An expectation is a boolean rule on a dataset, such as amount is not null. Its policy decides what happens to a row that breaks it. Warn, the default, keeps the row and records how many passed and failed. Drop removes the row. Fail stops the update. The documentation says metrics are tracked for warn and drop. When fail triggers, the update stops and is rolled back, so there are no metrics. I want to be honest about what the board shows. The SQL is documented, not run. The counts are local arithmetic that I computed over our eleven bronze events, applying each documented policy. They are not output from a pipeline engine. With warn, all eleven rows are kept, and the pass and fail counts are recorded per rule. With drop, eight rows are kept and three are dropped, orders seven, eight and nine. With fail, the update stops and nothing is written. Notice that order seven, with a null amount, fails both amount rules, because null is not greater than zero. Choose warn to measure first, drop when bad rows are expected, and fail when one bad row means the data cannot be trusted. One design point matters here. A dropped row simply disappears. If you need to look at it later, you need a quarantine dataset that receives the failures, so decide that before you choose drop. Next we look at what an update actually recomputes.

People assume that every dataset in a pipeline refreshes the same way, and it does not. A streaming table reads only new input. A materialized view is documented to refresh incrementally when the platform can, and otherwise to recompute, and which one it uses depends on the query, so you should not assume it. Here are four updates, with new rows of three, three, zero and two. For the streaming read, I use the local analogue from chapter four, where a file stream read exactly three, three, zero and two rows. The third update had nothing new, so the streaming table did no work. For the materialized view, I can only report what is documented, which is incremental or full, so check how your query refreshes before you depend on it. Now the important case, where the source itself changes. I tested this locally. I streamed from a Delta table, then updated a row in that table. The stream failed with an error called source table ignore changes, saying a data update was detected, which is not supported. If you set the option skip change commits, the stream carries on, but the update never arrives downstream. That is why a streaming table assumes its source is append only. If your source updates rows, you need a different design, which is exactly what the next section is for. Next we look at AUTO CDC.

Chapter six built a sequence guarded merge by hand: keep a record only if its sequence is newer, keep deletes as markers, and break ties with a second sort key. AUTO CDC lets you declare that instead. It applies a change feed to a target streaming table. You name the keys, which says what identifies a row. You say what to sequence by, which says which change is newer, and you choose whether to store the latest only, which is type one, or the full history, which is type two. Compare the definition with what we wrote by hand. The condition where the new sequence is greater than the stored one becomes the sequence by clause. Using a struct of several columns is documented for breaking ties, which matches our tie breaker. I would re-verify that clause. With type two, the target gets start at and end at columns, whose type matches the sequence column. I could not run any of this, so the small table is an illustration I built from the earlier events for order six. It is shaped like the documented output, and it was not produced by AUTO CDC. Choosing the key and the sequence column, and deciding whether a delete should close history, are still your decisions. You may also see this feature under older names, apply changes into in SQL and apply changes in Python. Those are the same idea under its previous spelling. The point is that the correctness rules from chapter six, ordering, ties, deletes and history, are now declared and managed. Next we see how updates and refreshes behave.

A pipeline can run in a few ways, and the difference between them is a matter of what gets reprocessed. A normal update processes new data. You can also refresh only selected tables, which saves time but can leave dependents stale. And a full refresh clears a table and rebuilds it by reading its sources again. All of this is documented, not run here. The danger of a full refresh is that it trusts the source. Take our order files. Files a, b and c hold three, three and two rows, so a full refresh rebuilds eight rows. But suppose file c has expired at the source, because the source only keeps files for a limited time. Then a full refresh can rebuild only six rows, and the two rows that came from file c are gone for good. That figure is simple arithmetic from the counts we measured in chapter four, not the result of a pipeline run. In chapter four we also saw what a lost checkpoint does without any truncation: the same files were appended again and the table doubled. A full refresh avoids the doubling because it also clears the table, but it still depends on what the source still has. To fix logic in one table, refresh that table and then its dependents. There is a documented guard. A table property called pipelines reset allowed, set to false, blocks a full refresh of that table. And the habit is to know the source's retention before you ever press the button. Next we look at the evidence a pipeline leaves.

Let's read the whole retail pipeline once, from the top, and then see what it leaves behind. Bronze orders is a streaming table that ingests the CSV files and keeps the source file name. Typed orders is a view that casts the text columns to real types. Silver orders is a streaming table fed by AUTO CDC, keyed on order id, sequenced by event time and source file, so that the latest event per order wins and ties are broken the way chapter five taught. And gold sales is a materialized view that sums the completed orders per store. All of this is documented, not run. Now the evidence. Every update writes an event log, which records updates starting and ending, the progress of each flow, data quality metrics and any errors, and you can query it like a table. The rows on the board are illustrative. I wrote them to show the kind of evidence an update leaves, and they were not captured from a real pipeline, so check the real schema in the documentation. How do you read a failure? Find the failed flow first. Then ask which kind of failure it is. A rule set to fail update means the data itself stopped the run. A source table ignore changes error, which we reproduced locally, means a streaming source was changed in place. Each leaves a different trail, and neither is fixed by restarting. A pipeline manages its internal dependencies. Next we coordinate it with other workloads and with upstream and downstream responsibilities.

A pipeline manages its own internal dependencies. But a real data product involves more than one pipeline, and that is what a job is for. A job runs tasks, and each task has a type. A notebook task runs Python or SQL logic. A pipeline task runs a declarative pipeline like the one in chapter seven. A SQL task runs a query on a warehouse. And a packaged code task runs a Python wheel or a JAR. The tasks form a directed acyclic graph, which means each task starts when the tasks it depends on allow it, and there are no cycles. As always in this chapter, the examples are documented, not run, because I had no workspace, and the field names should be checked against the live documentation. Here is the retail daily job. Ingest is a pipeline task over the landing files. Transform is SQL or a notebook that builds silver. Validate runs checks on silver, and publish writes gold. Each task names the task before it in its dependencies. A graph also means independent tasks can run side by side, and a failure stops only what depends on it. How do you choose a type? Use a pipeline for managed datasets, SQL for set logic, a notebook for code, and a wheel or JAR when the code is a tested package. Remember that the job only coordinates. The tasks do the work, and the work still has to be correct and safe to repeat. Next we look at how values move between tasks.

Jobs are reusable because their inputs are not hard coded. A job parameter is an input to a run, such as the run date. Inside a task you refer to it with a double brace reference to the job parameter. A task can also set a value for the tasks after it, called a task value, for example the number of rows it read, and a downstream task reads that value with a similar reference. I should be clear that the reference syntax here is documented, not run, and the exact spelling for task values is something to re verify. A condition task then compares a value and decides what runs. To see the flow, I ran a small local model of these rules, with real row counts. In the first run all three files were present, so ingest read eight rows and set rows read to eight. The condition said at least eight, which is true, so publish ran. In the second run, file c had not arrived. Ingest read six rows, the condition was false, and publish was excluded. Nothing was published from that short load, which is exactly the point.
