The condition turned a data problem into a controlled decision. The same idea handles environments. Development, staging and production should differ in their parameters, such as paths, catalogs and dates, and not in their code. Next we look at when jobs should start.

When should a job start? There are a few ways, all documented, not run here. A scheduled trigger starts the job at times you set with a cron expression. A file arrival trigger starts it when a new file lands in a storage location. A table update trigger starts it when an input table changes. And a continuous job runs all the time and restarts itself. The trade is freshness against compute. To make that concrete, suppose three files arrive a day. That is an assumption for illustration, not a measurement. An hourly schedule would run twenty four times a day, and most of those runs would find nothing new. A file arrival trigger would run three times, once per file. A nightly schedule would run once, and the results would be up to a day old. Watch for a burst of files, which can mean a burst of runs, and for a schedule so rare it breaks a freshness promise. None of those is automatically right. The consumer's freshness need, which we set in chapter one, decides. If finance reads a total at six in the morning, a nightly run is plenty. If a store dashboard needs fifteen minutes, an event trigger fits better. I am not quoting any prices. What each run actually costs is a measurement, and chapter nine returns to it. Next we look at what happens inside the graph when a task fails.

What happens to the rest of the graph when one task fails? By default, a task runs only if all the tasks it depends on succeeded. If an upstream task failed, the dependent task is skipped, which is different from failed. It simply did not run. You can change that with a run if condition. The documented options include all succeeded, which is the default, at least one succeeded, none failed, all done, at least one failed, and all failed. Here is one run, from a local model of those rules. Ingest succeeded. Transform failed once, from a transient fault that I injected. Validate and publish depend on transform, so both were skipped. I also added an alert task that depends on transform and has the run if condition at least one failed, and it ran and succeeded. That is a failure path: a task that exists to run when something else goes wrong. Jobs also have if else tasks, which branch on a value, and for each tasks, which loop over a list of inputs. A task whose condition was false also did not run, and that is a decision, not an error. There is a trap in the skipped status. A skipped task did not run, so it tells you nothing about whether its work would have been fine. Do not read skipped as checked and healthy. Next we look at how to recover from this failure.

There are three ways to recover, and each repeats a different amount of work. A retry runs one task again after it fails. A repair run runs only the unsuccessful tasks again, meaning the failed ones and the ones skipped because of them, and it keeps the results of tasks that already succeeded. A full rerun starts every task from the beginning. The documentation is explicit about one thing. The jobs system does not make tasks idempotent, so if a task wrote part of its output before failing, running it again can duplicate that output. I tested those ideas on a local model with real Delta tables. Transform failed once. A repair run re ran transform, validate and publish, but did not re run ingest, so bronze stayed at eight rows. A full rerun with an ingest that appends gave sixteen rows in bronze, the same eight rows twice. A downstream distinct step hid the duplicates, which is worse, because nothing complained. With an ingest that merges on the file and the order, the same full rerun left eight. Then retries. A publish task wrote its row, and then timed out. The retry wrote again. With an append, that left two published rows. With a merge on the run date, one. So choose a retry for a transient fault with no side effects, a repair when a middle task failed and the early ones are fine, and a full rerun when inputs or logic changed upstream. The misconception is that recovery is safe by construction. Only idempotent writes make it so, and that is a design decision. Next we look at who the job runs as.

A job does not run as whoever clicked run. It runs its tasks as one identity, which can be a user or a service principal, and every read and write is checked against that identity's privileges. The run as setting is documented, and I did not run it, so verify the details. We already have the identity for our example, from chapter two. The job runs as the etl runner service principal. In that chapter we gave it the right to read bronze and to read and write silver, and nothing on gold. So look at each task. Ingest writes bronze, which is allowed. Transform reads bronze and writes silver, which is allowed. Publish writes gold, and that is refused, because etl runner has no grants on the gold schema. The error on the board is the shape of a denial, not an exact message. I checked the logic against the chapter two permission model, which says exactly that. The fix follows least privilege. Grant use schema and modify on the gold schema, to that one principal, and nothing broader. Who may view, run or manage the job is a separate setting, and so is its owner. Do not fix it by running the job as a person with wide access, or by putting a person's credentials into code. Prefer a service principal, give it only what the tasks need, and remember that who clicks run does not change who the job runs as. Next we assemble a whole job.

Let's design the whole retail job so that any recovery is safe. We order the tasks by what each one needs. Ingest depends on nothing, and it writes bronze with a merge on the file name and the order id, so reading the same files twice changes nothing. Transform depends on ingest, and it overwrites silver, so running it again gives the same result. Validate depends on transform and only reads. Publish depends on validate, and on the row count condition from section two, and it merges on the run date, so a retry cannot add a second row. In the local model, run one had transform fail once. Ingest had succeeded, validate and publish were skipped, and the alert ran. Then a repair run re ran only transform, validate and publish. Ingest was not run again. The published table ended with one row, one hundred and sixty dollars, and bronze held eight rows. Because every task is safe to repeat, a full rerun would have given the same result, and that is what makes a failure boring. The rest of the checklist comes from this chapter. Run as a service principal with the least privileges. Put the environment in parameters. And let a condition stop publication when the load is short. Distinguish this from the exactly once business effects discussed earlier. The orchestration only repeats tasks. Your writes decide whether repeating is harmless. The work is coordinated. Next we inspect execution evidence and choose improvements that meet latency and cost requirements.

Chapter nine is about making things faster and cheaper, and the first rule is to check the answer before the speed. A baseline is the correct result of a representative workload, with a checksum. A change only counts as faster if the result stays the same, and a layout that changes the answer is wrong, not fast. Here is the baseline for this chapter, from a local run. I generated one million orders, with a hash based generator so the data is identical every time, and stored them five ways: with no layout, Z ordered, liquid clustered, partitioned by order date, and partitioned by customer. Every layout returned exactly one million rows and a sum of amount of fifty million four hundred ninety seven thousand four hundred thirty six dollars. That is the checksum every later comparison has to match. Then there are the limits of measurement. Compare like with like: the same data, the same query, and the same compute, and change one thing at a time. Timings vary from run to run, even on the same machine, so a single timing is an anecdote. For that reason, this chapter quotes counts you can repeat, such as files opened, rows per partition and tasks per stage, and it never quotes a timing. Next we look at how to find where the work goes.

Before you change anything, find where the work goes. A job is split into stages, and each stage into tasks. The Spark UI shows metrics for each of them, and the same numbers are available from its monitoring REST API. A healthy stage has tasks of similar size. A skewed stage has a few tasks doing most of the work, and the stage only ends when its slowest task ends. Here is a real excerpt from a local run. I made eighty percent of the orders belong to one store, then asked Spark to repartition by store, so that a shuffle stage with four tasks reads the data. The REST task summary reports how many records each task read, at five quantiles. The minimum is thirty six thousand, the lower quartile forty three thousand, the median sixty four thousand five hundred, and the upper quartile and maximum are both eight hundred fifty five thousand four hundred eighty. So one task read about thirteen times the median. That is the signature of skew, and it tells you where to look before you change anything. Read the quantiles: a maximum far above the median is skew, close together means even work, and rows and bytes are more repeatable evidence than time. On Databricks, the SQL query profile gives a similar per operator view, with rows and time, but I did not run it, so it is documented only. The habit is to read the evidence first and guess second. Next we look at sizing the compute itself.

Compute sizing comes down to whether the amount of parallelism fits the amount of data. Every shuffle partition becomes a task, and each task has overhead. Too many tiny tasks waste time, and too few leave machines idle. Here is a local example. I aggregated just one thousand rows. With two hundred shuffle partitions, which is Spark's default, the reduce stage ran two hundred tasks for one thousand rows. With four shuffle partitions it ran four tasks. And with two hundred partitions but adaptive query execution switched on, Spark coalesced the small partitions and ran a single task. So the right setting depends on the data, and adaptive execution can fix the common over partitioned case for you. Adding machines does not fix one slow task, so resize compute only after you have found the bottleneck. Then there are the platform choices. Photon is Databricks' vectorised engine, and serverless compute is managed for you, and both come with conditions: the kind of compute, the runtime, and which operators are supported. I did not run either, so I state them generically. Check that a feature is available in your workspace and applies to your workload, and then measure the difference. Never assume that a faster engine is faster for your query. Next we look at joins and skew.

Most of the cost of a join is moving data. Spark has two main strategies. A broadcast join sends a small table to every task, so the large table is not shuffled at all. A sort merge join shuffles both sides, so that matching keys land together. Here is a local run of orders joined to a table of fifty stores. By default, Spark chose a broadcast hash join, and the plan has one shuffle, which belongs to the group by afterwards. When I switched broadcasting off, the same query used a sort merge join with three shuffles, two for the join sides and one for the group by. The answer was identical. Only the data movement changed. Then skew. With eighty percent of the orders on one store, repartitioning one million rows into four partitions put eight hundred fifty five thousand rows in the largest one. Evenly spread data gave a largest partition of three hundred nineteen thousand. Adding a salt, which splits the hot key into sixty four pieces, brought the largest partition down to two hundred ninety nine thousand. Be careful with that trick. Salting adds a step and a second aggregation, so use it for a skew you have measured. And the cheapest speed up is often to filter and select before the join, so fewer rows enter it. Next we look at files.

Small files are one of the most common hidden costs. Every write task writes its own files. So many tasks, or a write that is split across many partitions, produces many small files. Each query then has to open and plan every one of them. The remedy is compaction, which on Delta tables is the optimize command: it rewrites small files into fewer, larger ones. Here are the numbers from a local run, on the same one million rows. Written by two hundred tasks, the table had one hundred twenty eight files. After optimize, it had twenty five. I lowered the target file size to four hundred kilobytes so that a small demo produces several files, as a big table would. The bigger surprise is partitioning. Partitioning the same rows by order date produced seven hundred twenty files, because each of the twenty four write tasks wrote a file into each of thirty partitions. Partitioning by customer, a column with a thousand values, produced two thousand files. Partitioning an unsorted write multiplies files. So look at files per partition and not only partitions, and partition only on a column with few, large values. There are trade-offs. Compaction rewrites data, so it costs compute and storage. And these counts are for this run and this layout, so they illustrate the effect and do not predict your numbers. Next we look at layouts that let a query skip files.

A layout is useful only for the filters it was built for, and the evidence in this section is the clearest in the chapter. Delta keeps the minimum and maximum value of each column for every file, so a query can skip files that cannot contain a match. For that to work, rows with similar values have to be stored together. Clustering does that, whether it is Z ordering or liquid clustering. Partitioning does something different: it puts rows into separate folders that a filter can prune. Here is the count of files opened by a query for store seven, in a local run on one million orders. With no layout, it opened all twenty four of twenty four files. Compaction alone gave two files, and the query still opened both, because compacting does not sort. After Z ordering by store, the table had nineteen files, and the same query opened one. Liquid clustering by store gave the same result, one of nineteen. But filter on customer instead, a column the layout was not built for, and both opened all nineteen. And the table partitioned by date opened all seven hundred twenty files, because the filter was not on the partition column. Cluster by the columns used in filters, partition only when each partition holds a lot of data, and with many access patterns expect to measure. So these are not interchangeable recipes. They differ in which filters they help, how they handle writes, and what they cost to maintain. Choose by the filters your table actually gets. Next we look at automating the upkeep.

The maintenance we have looked at, compacting files, removing old ones, and refreshing statistics, is routine, and routine work is a good candidate for automation. Databricks documents a feature for it called predictive optimization. I could not run it, so this is documented, not run, and it is based on summaries of the documentation. It runs optimize, which includes incremental clustering, vacuum, and analyze, on its own. It applies only to Unity Catalog managed tables, and it is not available in every region. It does not run Z ordering. And automatic liquid clustering, written as cluster by auto, is documented to need predictive optimization and a recent runtime. Whether it is switched on for you depends on your account. The documentation says it is on by default for accounts created after a date in November of twenty twenty four, with older accounts being moved over gradually, so check yours instead of assuming. Even with automation, some things stay with a person. Retention is a decision with consequences, as chapter three showed. Cost still needs reviewing. And someone has to check that the automation did what you expected, on the tables you care about. Next we bring it together in one worked comparison.

Let's finish by comparing the layouts on cost, with every assumption written down. The idea is simple. Cost is the work done multiplied by an assumed rate. The work, here the number of files a query opens, we measured in the last two sections. The rest is assumption, and the assumptions must be stated, because without them the numbers mean nothing. I assume it takes three seconds to open a file, that the job uses two machines, that a machine costs one unit per hour, and that the query runs twenty four times a day. None of these is a price or a measurement. With those assumptions, the unclustered table, which opens twenty four files, costs ninety six hundredths of a unit a day. Compaction alone, which opens two, costs eight hundredths. The table clustered by store, which opens one, costs four hundredths. And the table partitioned by date, which opens seven hundred twenty files for this filter, costs twenty eight point eight units a day. The ratios are real consequences of the file counts, but the sizes are only as good as the assumptions. Scan time is not really proportional to the number of files, and rewriting the table to cluster it is a real cost that this table does not show. A measured comparison on your workload is the only honest one. Performance changes must survive deployment and failure. Next we connect development, access, monitoring and recovery into an operational process.

The last chapters of this course are about running a data product for a long time, and the first habit is to structure the project so that most of its logic can be tested without a workspace. The idea is simple. Write the transformations as pure functions over data frames, in a package, with no reading or writing inside them. Keep the reading, writing and scheduling in thin job code that calls those functions. And keep everything, the code and the deployment definition, in Git. This is a real project, in the examples folder of this repository. It holds the chapter five transformations in one file, with no input or output. Its tests run on local Spark, with no workspace. And a job definition and a bundle file say what to deploy and where. Think about the boundary between local and remote. A notebook is a good place to explore, but logic that is worth testing belongs in a function. And a local run can cover the logic only. Permissions, scale and scheduling show up only in a workspace, which is why the later sections use bundles and several environments. I should say that the bundle files here are documented, not validated, because validating one needs a workspace to sign in to. Next we look at how code is packaged.

Once the code is in a package, the next question is what to put in it. A wheel is a built Python package that a job can install. The most important rule is to declare only the dependencies that your code needs, and to leave out what the runtime already provides. Spark is provided by the runtime, so pinning it in your wheel can fight with the version that the runtime brings. I built the example project's wheel locally with pip, so this is real. The file is called retail etl, version zero point one point zero, and it contains the transform module and an entry point. Its metadata lists no dependency on pyspark. The only requirement it names is pytest, and only as an extra for testing, which is not installed in production. Locally, my virtual environment provides pyspark, pinned to the version I tested with. On a workspace, the runtime provides it. The compatibility habits are documented, not run. Test on the runtime version you deploy to, because a library that works on one runtime can break on another. Pin what only your code uses. And isolate the environments of different jobs, so that an upgrade for one cannot break another. Next we look at tests.

Tests are how a pipeline earns the right to change. There are three layers, and each guards a different risk. A unit test checks one function on a small input and compares exact rows. An integration test runs the whole flow and checks each layer. And data quality tests assert properties that the output must always have, whatever the input. The example project has seven tests, and I ran them: seven passed. Four are unit tests, covering typing the columns, naming the failing rule, keeping the latest event per order with its tie breaker, and showing that a duplicate store key inflates a total. One integration test checks that eleven events become six silver orders and three quarantined rows, with a gold total of one hundred seventy. Two data quality tests check that silver has one row per order and no null amounts, and that gold equals the silver detail. Each layer catches something the others miss: unit tests are fast and pinpoint the function, integration tests catch wiring, and quality tests catch data nobody anticipated. Then there is the quality of a failure. I wrote a deliberately buggy variant that sorts ascending, so the oldest event wins, and ran it through the same comparison. Instead of a bare assertion error, it said what was missing, order six completed from file d, and what was unexpected, order six pending from file b. A failing test that names the wrong row is worth a lot at three in the morning. Next we look at declaring where code deploys.

A bundle turns deployment into a file in Git. It is a configuration file, called databricks dot yml, that names the resources to create, such as jobs and pipelines, the artifacts to build, such as a wheel, and the targets, which are your environments. When you deploy, the tool creates or updates exactly what the file declares. The current name is Declarative Automation Bundles. Older material calls them Databricks Asset Bundles, or DABs, and I mention that only so you recognise it. I wrote the example bundle for our project, but it is documented, not validated. The field names follow the documentation as I could check it through search summaries, and validating a bundle needs a workspace to sign in to, which I did not have. The abridged file on the board has a name, an include line that pulls in the job definition from the resources folder, and two targets. The dev target is in development mode. The prod target is in production mode, and it runs as a service principal. The commands are validate, which checks the configuration, deploy, which creates or updates the resources, and run, which starts a job. A bundle does not check your data or your logic, and it does not move data between environments. Deployment intent lives in the file, so a review of the file is a review of the deployment. Next we look at moving it through environments.

A change should travel from a developer's laptop to production the same way every time. In a bundle, each environment is a target. On a pull request, the tests run, and the bundle is validated against staging. When the change is merged, the bundle is deployed to staging and the job is exercised there. Then the same file is deployed to production. The sketch on the board is a sketch of a pipeline, not a validated one. The documentation describes what the modes do. Development mode prefixes resource names with the deployer and marks them as development, so developers do not collide. Production mode adds checks at deploy time, including that the git branch matches the target, and the documentation recommends running production under a service principal. Before promotion, tests and validate run on every pull request, and staging runs the real job before production does. How do you roll back? You redeploy the previous commit, which is one more reason deployment lives in git. But be careful, because that is a rollback of code, not of data. If a bad version already wrote bad rows, redeploying the old code does not remove them. That needs its own recovery, using the tools from chapters three and six, such as restore and replay. Know that difference before the day you need it. Next we look at seeing what a running system is doing.

When something looks wrong in production, the first skill is knowing where to look. A running system leaves several kinds of evidence. Logs say what ran. Metrics say how much. Lineage says what feeds what. Audit records say who did what. And billing records say what it cost. Databricks exposes some of this through system tables, which you can query with SQL. This is documented, not run, and the table names should be re checked. Match each question to its source. If you ask what a particular run did, look at the job and task logs. If you ask what each flow in a pipeline read, look at the pipeline event log from chapter seven. If you ask what feeds a table, use lineage, which chapter two introduced. If you ask who touched a table, use the audit records. And to ask what a job cost, the billing usage system table has a custom tags column and a usage metadata struct with the job id, so you can sum the usage quantity by job over the last week, as the query shows. The documentation confirms that table. The habits that help are to name the question before opening a log, to tag jobs so cost and ownership can be found, and to use lineage and audit records for investigations and not only for audits. There are caveats. System tables must be enabled for your account and granted to you, and the exact names and columns for the others should be checked against the live documentation. Next we turn evidence into objectives and alerts.

Chapter one began with what consumers need, and now we can turn that into objectives we can measure. An objective is a promise a consumer cares about, with a threshold. You measure it, and you alert when it is breached. Take two, using the eleven events from chapter five. A freshness objective might say that the newest event must be under fifteen minutes old. I computed it against a fixed clock of ten twenty, so the result is repeatable. The newest event was at nine fifty, so thirty minutes old, and the objective is breached. A quality objective might say that at least ninety five percent of events pass the rules. Eight of the eleven passed, which is seventy two point seven percent, and that is breached too. The thresholds are illustrative choices, but the measurements are real computations. Think about how to alert. Alert on the objective, not on every error, so that one breach produces one alert. Say who is paged and what to check first. And treat a breach as the start of a diagnosis, not as a signal to rerun the job. As chapter eight showed, a blind rerun can duplicate data. Look at the evidence from the last section first, then decide on a repair, a replay or a fix. Next we look at recovery and at deleting data on purpose.

Recovery has a mirror image, which is deleting data on purpose, and the lesson is that deleting is not one command. I demonstrated this in a local run. I made a small table of orders with the change feed on, and a derived table holding the total spend, computed before the delete. Then I deleted customer c1's rows. The current table no longer has them. But look at where the data still lives. An older version of the table still returned c1's rows when I read it. The change feed still returned c1's rows, with their values, as delete records. And the derived table still said one hundred dollars, which counts c1. Then I vacuumed with a retention of zero hours, which I can only do on a throwaway table. Reading the old version and the change feed now failed, because the files were gone. But the derived table was untouched, still one hundred, because vacuum only cleans the files of the table it runs on. Only recomputing it brought the total down to thirty five. Recovery has the same shape. A backfill re reads history, so it needs idempotent writes. Checkpoints hold offsets and state, so protect them. And source retention limits any replay. So a deletion obligation is a checklist. Delete at the source of truth, vacuum once your retention allows, recompute every derived table, and check change feeds, checkpoints and any copies. And remember that the retention period decides when the data is truly gone. Next we look at secrets and identities.

Production needs credentials, and handling them badly is one of the easiest ways to cause an incident. A secret should be read at run time from a secret store, and never written in code, in git, or in a log. In a notebook or job you read it with a call to get a secret from a scope and a key. The documentation says its value is redacted in output, but I could not run it, so verify that. Then there are identities. A service principal is an identity for automation. And it helps to separate three roles. The service principal that runs your continuous integration deploys the bundle. It needs to manage the job, and it needs no access to the data at all. The run as principal runs the job. It needs to read and write the tables the job uses, as the run as example in chapter eight showed, and nothing more. And a person reviews and approves changes, with view access, rather than using production credentials for day to day work. Each has the least it needs. The trace on the board is illustrative, not a real error message. It shows the shape of a failure when a credential has expired or been revoked: the deploy fails with an authentication error, and the data is untouched. So rotate credentials on a schedule, and alert before they expire. Next we put owners on all of this.

A control that nobody owns fails silently, so the last step is to name owners and the evidence they use. Here is a proposal for the retail data product. Pipeline code belongs to data engineering, and its evidence is the git history. Deployment belongs to the continuous integration service principal, with the deploy log as evidence. The quality objective belongs to the product owner, who watches the quality metrics. And cost belongs to the team lead, who uses billing records grouped by tag, so each job's spend has a team. Capacity is how much work fits in the schedule window, and tags let spend map to an owner. That is a design proposal, not a standard. Now an incident, with assumed numbers, to show why detection time matters. Suppose the source keeps its files for seven days. On day zero, ingestion fails, and there is no alert. On day five, finance notices a gap. Now we are five days behind, and only two days of replay window remain. On day six it is fixed and the backfill starts, with one day left. If it had been noticed on day eight, day zero's data would have expired at the source and been lost. The numbers are hypothetical, but the arithmetic is the point: the replay window shrinks every day you do not notice. So alert on freshness, and know your retention. Individual controls are now connected. Next we assess a complete data product under changed requirements and realistic failures.

We now have every piece of a retail data product, so let's explain why each piece is there. The most useful habit in design review is to name where each guarantee comes from. A guarantee always comes from somewhere specific. It can come from storage, from processing, from orchestration, from governance, or from the external source. If you cannot say which, you are probably claiming more than the design delivers. Look at the retail design from chapters one to ten. The order files come with a contract and a retention. Bronze keeps what arrived, with the source file. Silver is typed, keyed, and the latest event wins. Gold is a summary per store, which started at one hundred seventy dollars. And the consumers are finance and the dashboard. Now the guarantees. Atomic commits and history come from storage, the Delta tables. One row per order comes from processing, a keyed merge with a sequence guard. Order of execution and retries come from orchestration, a job. Who may read comes from governance, the grants. And how far back you can replay comes from the source's own retention, not from anything we built. Ask of every component which guarantee it provides, and what happens if it fails. The misconception to avoid is that the platform makes the whole thing exactly once. Each guarantee has an owner, and some of them are not ours. A note on status: Unity Catalog, Auto Loader, pipelines and jobs were documented in this course, not run. Next we change the requirements.

Requirements will change, and a good design absorbs a change in one place, with evidence that it still reconciles. I applied three changes to the same retail design in a local run, reusing the real example package. The first is a historical correction. A later file says that order four was actually eighteen dollars, not fifteen. In the design, a correction is just a later event, so the latest event wins. York becomes eighteen dollars, and the total becomes one hundred seventy three. The history keeps both versions of order four, the fifteen dollar version closed by the eighteen dollar one. The second change is a new source. A partner sends orders with store codes instead of store ids, and one of the codes is unknown. We map the codes onto the common shape and let the quality rules reject what does not map. Two of the three partner orders load, the third is quarantined, and the total becomes two hundred fifteen. The third change is latency. I applied the same logic as three micro batches, each a merge guarded by a sequence, and the result was identical to the full recompute. The design held because a correction is a later event and not an edit in place, and a new source is mapped and not special cased. Finally, reconcile. Fifteen input rows equal eight silver orders, plus three older versions, plus four quarantined rows. Next we compare the ways of building this.

There are three broad ways to build the retail flow, and the useful comparison is who carries the work. With jobs and notebooks, you write every step yourself, including the merge, and you are responsible for making retries safe. You get the most control and carry the most. With declarative pipelines, you write the datasets and the rules, and the platform works out the order and manages the state. With managed ingestion, you name the source and the destination, and the connector reads and tracks its own progress. As always, this comparison is documented, not run. None of them is best. Each fits a situation, and the more the platform carries, the less you write and the less you control. Each still leaves something to you: idempotency and state with jobs, keys, sequence and rules with pipelines, and source limits and governance with managed ingestion. A defensible choice for the retail example might combine them. Use managed ingestion for the source if the source is supported. Use a declarative pipeline for silver and gold, where keyed merges and quality rules are declared. Use a job to order the work, to guard publication with a condition, and to alert. And keep ordinary code only for what is genuinely custom. Notice that this is a reasoned choice, not a rule. If the source is not supported, or you need unusual parsing, the answer changes, and you should be able to say why. Next we critique the design against failures.

A design review should attack the design. For each realistic failure, ask three questions. What is the first sign? What guards against it? And what evidence shows that the guard works? Then list what is still unguarded. Take four failures, with evidence from earlier chapters. First, missing data. If file c never arrives, a row count condition keeps the publish task from running, and nothing is published from a short load. That evidence came from the chapter eight model. Second, duplicates. If order four is sent twice, keyed latest wins, with a tie breaker, keeps one row, and chapter five tested that with twelve shuffles. Third, drift. In chapter four, the text twelve comma fifty was read as twelve hundred fifty, silently, with no error. The guard is type rules with a quarantine, and the lesson is that it failed quietly, so the rules must be there before the data arrives. Fourth, access loss. If the run as principal loses a grant, the job is refused. The fix is a least privilege grant, as chapters two and eight showed. Now be honest about what is unguarded. A decimal comma can still pass a fixed schema. An alert that nobody reads is not a guard. And a source can expire before you replay. Naming the gaps is part of the design. Next we write down the decisions.

The last thing a design needs is a written record of its decisions. A decision record says what was chosen, what was rejected and why, what the choice guarantees, what it assumes about cost, and what risks remain open. Here are four entries for the retail design. We chose a keyed merge into silver, instead of appending and hoping, and it guarantees that replays are idempotent. We chose slowly changing dimension type two for orders, instead of overwriting, so that history survives corrections like the one we saw. We chose to cluster the gold table by store, instead of partitioning by date, because the measurements in chapter nine showed far fewer files opened for a store filter. And we chose to run as a service principal, not a person, for least privilege. Revisit the record whenever a requirement, a source or a platform feature changes. Now the honest part, the unresolved risks. Large parts of this design were documented in this course and not run: Unity Catalog, Auto Loader, declarative pipelines and Jobs. The cost figures are assumptions, not measurements, and no price was quoted anywhere. Platform wording needs checking against the live documentation. And the retention of each real source is something you have to confirm. Reading this course explains how such a design is built and why. It does not show that anyone reading it can build one, and I make no claim that it does. Continue with unfamiliar sources and operating scenarios, and deepen practical competence through separate implementation experience and feedback.
